one_pager.big_idea: Even a simple-sounding claim can be hard to test: scientists must agree exactly what they will measure (an operational definition), and different definitions, or different conditions, can give different answers.
goals: I can carry out a fair test of the claim 'Hot water freezes faster than cold water' (Plan A) or compare the cooling of hot and warm water (Plan B), and record my results.
I can explain what an operational definition is, show how the choice of definition can change a verdict, and say what my evidence can and cannot show.

flow.what: Three retrieval questions answered on the back of the worksheet: the control group in the lucky pen trial (Code 52), what to measure, and what 'frozen' means (write several answers on the board and keep them). Teacher checks the kit trays and, in Plan A, the freezing mixtures. Slides 1 to 2.
The Mpemba story (Tanzania, 1963; Mpemba and Osborne, 1969; a 2016 study found no clear effect; still contested). Vote: 'Do you think hot water can freeze faster?' Yes, No or Not sure. Slides 3 to 4.

Set-up explained (2 min); safety slide read in both languages (1 min); teacher fills the H tubes (Plan A) or the H and W cups (Plan B) and groups start timing (2 min); operational definitions taught (2 min) while Measurers keep reading. Plan A: three definitions of 'frozen'. Plan B: three definitions of 'cooling faster'. Slides 5 to 9 (A or B).

Plan A: thermometer tubes read every 30 seconds until 0 °C, then thermometers out; observation tubes checked every minute for first crystals and fully solid; Reporters take results to the board at minute 28; class tally, then Stretch. Plan B: both cups read every minute to 15 minutes (about minute 26), curves plotted as they go, 15-minute drops added to the class table. Slides 10 (A or B) and 11.

Debate with the class results (4 min): Plan A, did the winner change with the definition (concept cartoon, slide 12A); Plan B, does cooling faster at first prove freezing first (slide 12B). Two verdicts modelled: 'our test' and 'the claim in general' (slide 13). Exit ticket (3 min) and logbook line (1 min). Slides 12 to 14.

one_pager.practical: Plan A: each group puts four tubes with 3 ml of water (two warm, about 60 °C, and two cool) into an ice and salt freezing mixture at the same time, reads the thermometer tubes every 30 seconds until 0 °C and checks the observation tubes every minute for first crystals and fully solid. Plan B: each group reads cups of 100 ml of water at about 60 °C and about 35 °C every minute for 15 minutes and plots two cooling curves.
one_pager.assessment: Output: class results and the definition debate (Plan A), or two cooling curves and the limits-of-evidence debate (Plan B). Exit ticket: operational definition, two definitions of 'frozen', and a verdict with a reason. Logbook line under 'What I found'. Tracker: record each student's project group (Weeks 6 to 10) in column F.
hazards: Plan A: the ice and salt freezing mixture reaches about minus 10 to minus 18 °C and can cause a cold burn: gloves on, tubes handled by the top, fingers never in the mixture.
Plan A: salty splashes sting eyes: goggles on while the mixture is on the table; wash hands afterwards.
Warm water can scald: only the teacher prepares and pours it, no hotter than about 60 °C; cups and tubes of warm water stay on the tray and are not carried.
Glass thermometers break easily: never stir with one or pull one out of ice; if one breaks, step back and tell the teacher.
No eating or drinking; never taste the ice, salt or water.
Spills make floors slippery: wipe up at once.
one_pager.language_note: Frames: 'Our operational definition of frozen is ___.' 'Using this definition, the ___ water froze first.' 'The data suggests ___; however, ___.' 'Our evidence cannot show ___ because ___.' 'Our verdict is ___ because ___.' Chinese talk is welcome in the Hook vote, during predictions and in the definition debate; readings are called out in English ('minus two degrees', 'two point five minutes'). Traps: 'frozen' in everyday speech means 'very cold'; 'cool' can mean 'lower in temperature' or 'good'; 'freezing point' is a temperature, not a moment in time; say negative temperatures as 'minus three degrees'. Year 9: key words are bilingual, instructions are in English.
watch_out: Run ONE plan only, from the handover note (field 7). If the ice is late or does not arrive, switch to Plan B: hide the Plan A slides and hand out Version B.
A freezing mixture that warms up is the most common problem: top it up with ice and a spoonful of salt halfway through. Mixed results between groups are not a failure: they are the lesson.
'Hot water must freeze first because it cools faster': it cools faster at first, but it also has further to go.
'Water always freezes at exactly 0 °C': water can supercool a few degrees below 0 °C before the first crystals form.

If time is short: Plan A, drop the 'first crystals' checks and record 'not solid at ___ min' if tubes are not solid by minute 30; Plan B, stop at 10 minutes. Cut Challenge; keep the definition debate and the verdict.

Bring the Week 3 ruler-drop cards and the Week 4 class data photo in case groups choose claims 12 or 9. Read the exit tickets and enter project groups in tracker column F first.

open_questions: Schema: 'plan' is fixed at 'Both' for Year 9, but Y9_W06_The_Mpemba_mystery.md has a Plan A / Plan B switch with different worksheets, kit and prep. Plan-specific rows are marked 'Plan A:' or 'Plan B:' at the start of the item or task; rows with no prefix are needed in both plans. Totals must not add both plans together.

Worksheet page counts: the lesson file gives none. The designed Version A has 3 pages and Version B has 4 (design/export_all/sites/Y9_W06_printables/project), both entered as 2 double-sided sheets. In Version B there is no blank back for the Do Now ('answer on the back of the worksheet'), and cutting off the exit ticket strip on page 4 also cuts the foot of page 3. Print Version B's last sheet single-sided, or collect the whole worksheet?

Backup copies: the lesson file says 'Print a few copies of Version B every time', but a whole-class switch to Plan B needs 24 copies, the Plan B method cards, 12 identical 200 ml cups, a second jug and a 100 ml measuring jug. The file calls the Plan B kit 'a subset of the Plan A kit', but the Plan A kit list has none of these cups or jugs. How many backup copies, and should the Plan B kit be set aside in Plan A?
No worksheet spares are stated (24 copies, 1 per student). Add spares?

Small tubes: the kit card gives 4 per group (24, counted at clean-up) but the Teacher Guide Section 8 says '12 to 24 small tubes'. The kit card says glass thermometers; the Teacher Guide safety table says 'plastic tubes if possible' (Plan A) and 'spirit or digital thermometers' (Plan B). Which tubes and thermometers will be used?
Tubes must be marked at 3 ml and labelled H1, C1, H2, C2, and Plan B cups labelled H and W, but no marker pen or labels are in the kit list.
Version B needs pencils, and the cooling curves are plotted on a grid, but the Plan B kit card lists no pencils or other stationery. Do students bring their own?

Dry run: the notes for the incoming teacher ask for a dry run of the Plan A set-up the day before, but ice is arranged only 'on the day' (2 to 3 kg). No amount of ice or time is given for the dry run (25 minutes entered as an estimate).
Salt: the kit card lists 1 kg under 'Teacher'; 6 groups at about 100 g use about 600 g per class, plus top-ups and the dry run. Is 1 kg per class or in total?
Gloves: 2 pairs per group 'plus spares on the teacher's desk'; the number of spares and the sizes are not stated. Paper towel quantity is not stated.
Class results board: 'print both versions and use the one for the plan in use' means one A3 sheet per class is wasted; slide 11 shows the same table. Print only the version for the plan in use?

Concept cartoon (6 per class): it shows the Plan A debate (slide 12A) and the Plan A timeline lists it. The Plan B timeline is 'the same as Plan A except' and replaces the debate with slide 12B, so it is unclear whether the cartoon is printed in Plan B.

Method cards and kit card: the print spec is 6 method cards per class, laminated if possible (entered as one reusable set of 6). The kit card designs are marked 'Teacher copy', but the Teacher Guide has each group's Safety Officer check the kit card at the start of the Do phase. Print group copies of the kit card?

Plan A prep time: the kit card gives 'about 25 minutes' for collecting ice, marking tubes, mixing the freezing mixtures and making warm water. It is split here into four estimated tasks (8 + 7 + 6 + 4); marking the tubes is needed once, the rest for each class. Collecting kit, printing and the dry run are extra and have no stated times.

Project groups 'may be the same or re-formed in Week 6' (Teacher Guide) and go in tracker column F, but the lesson file gives no time or step for forming groups. The file also does not say whether worksheets are collected as rubric evidence (Weeks 6 to 9 worksheets support strands 1 to 5) or kept by students.

Timing: the Plan A slide 10A timeline has observation checks 'to about 16 min' and the sample data has tubes fully solid at 12 to 16 minutes after the start (about minute 9 of the lesson), which is close to minute 28 when results go to the board. Slide 13's icon says 'only 20 minutes'.
